Model identity

Every figure below is read from a declared artifact. This report fits nothing, loads no booster, recomputes no prediction and calls no betting optimiser.

Probit Offset is not the production model.

It is one of the standard published architectures, measured against the market on the same races as every other report here. Nothing in it is a promotion decision, and the promotion gates it can and cannot satisfy are in the technical appendix.

How each evaluation year was fitted

These are walk-forward figures rather than one model's: the model is refitted for each evaluation year on the seasons before it, so the result concatenates 11 separately fitted models and no evaluation year's outcomes appear in its own fit. This run did not record the year its training window starts, so this report does not name one.

Deltas in this report use model_minus_market_log_loss: race_multinomial_log_loss, where negative is better. That is stated because three delta fields existed in this repository and they did not all point the same way.

Provenance -- the source commit, the config and data digests, the environment and every input this report read by content digest -- is in the technical appendix and in run_lock.json beside this file. Canonical publication fails without it.

Probit Offset is better than the market by 0.004358 race_multinomial_log_loss on 7,933 races. The direction holds in 10 of 11 evaluated years. There is also a paired diagnostic against softmax_offset, which holds everything but one change fixed: on that comparison the delta is -0.000943. Every seed agrees on the sign of that paired delta.

Evaluation population and market reference

The market reference

Every metric below is reported beside the market's own implied probabilities on the same races, normalised within each race, and the delta is this model's race log loss minus the market's on the same races. One yardstick across every published report, so their headline numbers mean the same thing and can be read against one another. The market is a measurement, not a model this one is defined against.

The evaluation population

Every figure in this report covers the standardized evaluation window, which begins in 2016. One window for every published report, so their headline numbers are computed on the identical race keys and can be compared -- which is checked by digest before anything is published, not asserted in a footnote. 2015 is earlier than the window and is excluded from every evaluation figure below, including the bankroll paths. The feature-effect grid is the one exception, and says so where it appears: a learned response direction is a property of each year's fit rather than of the evaluation population.

Some years are warm-up rather than evaluation

2015 had no earlier year to fit a utility scale on and took the predeclared theoretical value (insufficient_history). The utility is divided by that scale, so those years amplify corrections where a fitted scale halves them, and their stakes and claimed edges are several times any fitted year's. They are excluded from every figure in this report and named here rather than labelled and left in.

Top-choice movement

Not applicable to this model. Top-choice movement needs the market's own first pick beside the model's, and this run's artifacts do not carry it. The paired diagnostic in the appendix holds the mean utilities fixed, which is a different and narrower question.

Ensemble stability

Not applicable to this model. There is no ensemble to be stable. This architecture is one choice link applied to one set of mean utilities, not a bag of independently fitted members, so seed variation here is integration noise rather than model disagreement -- and that is reported in the appendix instead.

Feature and correction effects

Not applicable to this model. There are no per-feature effects belonging to this model to attribute. A choice link changes how utilities become probabilities; it has no features of its own. The mean utilities are another run's fit, so attributing their feature effects here would credit this model with that run's work -- and for the market-anchored architecture they are the Softmax Offset margins exactly, whose per-feature effects, response directions and group ablation are in that report. What is specific to this model is the link and its utility scale, and both are in the technical appendix.

Betting and bankroll analysis

Retrospective odds

Every stake, return and bankroll figure in this report is computed against historical result-page odds and official dividends. Those are not an executable pre-race price: they are the prices after the pool closed, and a bet placed at them could not have been placed. Nothing here establishes profitability. A profitability claim requires a locked model shadow-tested against timestamped pre-race odds snapshots.

Do not select a threshold from these returns.

Every year through 2026 has been used as development data in this repository: features were searched, architectures compared and thresholds inspected against these same seasons. The chronological split is real, so a test year is genuinely after its training rows, but no test year is unseen. Treat the forward figures as probability progress rather than as a locked out-of-sample result, and do not select a Kelly level or an edge threshold from this reused history. The confirmation step that this run cannot substitute for is a prospective shadow test against archived pre-race price snapshots.

Probit Offset is not the production model, and this is not a proposal to stake it.

A settled ledger measures what a probability was worth economically, which is a different question from which model should carry money. That decision is the production model's, and the comparison that would inform it is in the technical appendix rather than in this table.

Settlement by staking rule

RoleWhat it is for
Primarywhat an operator would run: sized for the rebate, and credited it.
Sizing referencethe same settlement, sized blind. It isolates sizing for the cliff from receiving the rebate -- this row and the primary settle identically and differ only in what the solver knew.
Settlement ablationblind sizing with the rebate not credited. It isolates the rebate's own contribution to the return.
Benchmarka fixed flat stake above an edge floor, sized from the opening bankroll and never resized. Not a Kelly fraction, so it belongs to no preset panel below -- and it has no ruin stop, so a model that finds edge in most races can stake more than the bankroll holds and finish below zero. That is the yardstick behaving as defined rather than a settlement error: it is here to show what indiscriminate staking on this model's edges would have done, which is why it is a benchmark and not a proposal.

The check that matters most in this section: if the realised return in each edge bucket does not track the expected one, the edge estimate is wrong and every stake sized from it is wrong with it. The bucket counts are small enough that one winner moves a bucket, so read the pattern across buckets rather than any single number.

A negative-edge bucket appears only under rebate-aware sizing, and only at the larger fractions. That is the rule working as defined rather than a filter failing: the rebate is a cliff, so a runner whose own edge is negative can pay for itself by pushing the race's turnover over the threshold, and the stakes only get large enough for that at the higher fractions.

These are walk-forward figures rather than one model's: the model is refitted for each evaluation year on the seasons before it, so the result concatenates 11 separately fitted models and no evaluation year's outcomes appear in its own fit. This run did not record the year its training window starts, so this report does not name one. Each path is rebased on its own opening balance, so zero means break-even for every line from the same point. These curves are drawn from a bounded 998-point subsequence of up to 4,026 staked races, keeping each interval's highest and lowest balance so no peak or drawdown is smoothed away, and keeping the first and last points exactly. Every figure in the tables is computed from the full settlement, and the complete per-race path is in <code>race_paths.parquet</code>. Where a year is excluded, a continuous path opens at the balance the bank held when the kept years begin and an annual-reset path opens at the declared bankroll, so the two show different opening figures for the same rule. Rebate policy: 10% of the race net loss, once that loss reaches HK$10,000, as a cliff. Flat staking is omitted from these panels. Its stake is a fixed amount per bet and this settlement never halts on ruin, so its path can pass below zero -- a measure of how badly a rule loses rather than a balance an account could hold. It is also not a Kelly fraction, so it belongs to no preset. Its settlement is in the strategy table above. 2015 is excluded from every path below. These test years have no earlier year to fit the utility scale on and fall back to the predeclared theoretical value. The utility is divided by the scale, so the fallback amplifies corrections where a fitted scale halves them: their stakes and claimed edges are several times any fitted year's and are not comparable with them. Exclude these years from any return figure -- filter on is_honest_scale in the per-run CSV.

A day-block bootstrap: race days are resampled within each test year, so the interval accounts for clustering within a meeting, and the interval lies entirely below zero. It conditions on the fitted model and does not include refit uncertainty.

What a simulation cannot tell you

The model-assumed simulation draws winners from the model's own probabilities. If those probabilities are wrong the simulation is confidently wrong in the same direction, so it bounds sampling risk and says nothing about model risk.

Technical appendix and provenance

The utility scale

Fitted minimum
1.9932
Fitted maximum
2.2280
Theory
0.7797
the value theory predicts

The fitted scale sits above the value theory predicts, in every year: 1.993 to 2.228 against 0.780 (the scale the fallback year used, which is the predeclared theoretical value). Theory gets this wrong and the fit is what the report uses -- a scale asserted from theory would divide the utilities by too little, and at that value the market-relative candidate loses instead of winning. A run that took the theoretical value on faith would have reported the wrong sign, which is why the first year -- which has no history and falls back to it -- is excluded from the headline and labelled.

What this comparison holds fixed: the correction. It is the incumbent's persisted margin, reused exactly rather than refitted, and the market anchor means a zero correction returns the market probability -- so the only difference is the link. A diagnostic, not an identity. This report's headline is the market delta, because that is the one quantity every published report can be compared on. This delta answers a narrower question and answers it better -- it is the only measurement that separates one change from everything else -- and read as a headline it would mislead, because a model can beat the reference it holds fixed and still lose to the market.

Limitations and the retrospective-odds warning

Retrospective odds, restated

Every stake, return and bankroll figure in this report is computed against historical result-page odds and official dividends. Those are not an executable pre-race price: they are the prices after the pool closed, and a bet placed at them could not have been placed. Nothing here establishes profitability. A profitability claim requires a locked model shadow-tested against timestamped pre-race odds snapshots.

Restated at the end as well as beside the betting numbers, deliberately. It is the single most load-bearing caveat in this report and the one a reader skimming for a return figure is most likely to miss.

Every test year is also development data

Every year through 2026 has been used as development data in this repository: features were searched, architectures compared and thresholds inspected against these same seasons. The chronological split is real, so a test year is genuinely after its training rows, but no test year is unseen. Treat the forward figures as probability progress rather than as a locked out-of-sample result, and do not select a Kelly level or an edge threshold from this reused history. The confirmation step that this run cannot substitute for is a prospective shadow test against archived pre-race price snapshots.

What else this report does not establish

  • It measures Probit Offset against the market on the same races. It does not measure this model against the other published models except through that shared yardstick.
  • Its intervals condition on the fitted model, so they bound sampling risk and not model risk.
  • Every figure is out of sample in time but in sample in design: the feature set, the hyperparameters and the staking rules were all chosen with these years visible.
  • Nothing here is a shadow test. A profitability claim needs a locked model run forward against timestamped pre-race prices.
